'''Antonín Baudyš''' (9 September 1946 &ndash; 24 August 2010) was a [[Czechs|Czech]] academic and politician who served as defense minister from 1993 to 1994. He was the first defense minister of [[the Czech Republic]].<ref name=Ulrich1999>{{cite book|author=Marybeth Peterson Ulrich|title=Democratizing Communist Militaries: The Cases of the Czech and Russian Armed Forces|url=http://www.press.umich.edu/pdf/0472109693-03.pdf|year=1999|publisher=University of Michigan Press|isbn=978-0-472-10969-2|page=85}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Baudyš was born in [[Prague]] on 9 September 1946.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Brokl|first=Lubomir|author2=Zdenka Mansfeldová|title=Czech Republic|journal=European Journal of Political Research|date=December 1994|volume=26|issue=3–4|pages=269–277|doi=10.1111/j.1475-6765.1994.tb00446.x}}</ref><ref name=eiwire/> He studied mechanical engineering<ref name=Ulrich1999/> and graduated from [[Czech Technical University in Prague|the Czech Technical University]] (CVUT).<ref name=eiwire/>

==Career==
Baudyš worked as a university professor at his alma mater, CVUT, until 1989.<ref name=Ulrich1999/><ref name=eiwire/> He became a member of [[Czechoslovak People's Party|the Czechoslovak People's Party]] (CSL) in 1970.<ref name=eiwire/> He was named deputy prime minister in 1989 shortly after the fall of communist regime and held the post until July 1992.<ref name=eiwire/> He was appointed defense minister to [[Václav Klaus' First Cabinet|the coalition cabinet]] led by Prime Minister [[Václav Klaus]] in January 1993.<ref>{{cite book|author=Andrew A. Michta|title=America's New Allies: Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic in NATO|url=https://archive.org/details/americasnewallie00mich|url-access=registration|date=1 January 1999|publisher=University of Washington Press|isbn=978-0-295-80376-0|page=[https://archive.org/details/americasnewallie00mich/page/135 135]}}</ref> The ministry was formed with his appointment.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Vesselin Dimitrov|author2=Klaus H. Goetz|author3=Hellmut Wollmann|title=Governing After Communism: Institutions and Policymaking|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6zMLJe-jsUsC&pg=PA131|year=2006|publisher=Rowman & Littlefield|isbn=978-0-7425-4009-5|page=131}}</ref> He was a member of [[Christian Democratic Union - Czechoslovak People's Party|the Christian Democratic Union-Czechoslovak People's Party]] (KDU-CSL).<ref>{{cite news|title=Sacked Defense Minister Opens Old Wounds|url=http://www.praguepost.com/archivescontent/17004-sacked-defense-minister-opens-old-wounds.html|newspaper=The Prague Post|date=28 September 1994|author=Tomas Kellner|archiveurl=https://archive.today/20130826072008/http://www.praguepost.com/archivescontent/17004-sacked-defense-minister-opens-old-wounds.html|archivedate=26 August 2013}}</ref> On 22 September 1994, [[Vilém Holáň]] of KDU-CSL replaced Baudyš in the post.<ref>{{cite book|author=Jeffrey Simon|title=NATO Enlargement and Central Europe: A Study in Civil-military Relations|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cS8TIsg1Kg4C&pg=PA221|year=1996|publisher=DIANE Publishing|isbn=978-1-4289-8158-4|page=221}}</ref>

Following his removal from office, he worked as a businessman<ref>{{cite news|title=Czechs Say They Warned U.S. of Chemical Weapons in Gulf|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/10/19/us/czechs-say-they-warned-us-of-chemical-weapons-in-gulf.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm|newspaper=The New York Times|date=19 October 1996|author=Philip Shenon}}</ref> and a popular astrologist.<ref name=eiwire/>

===Activities===
One of his first activities as defense minister was to initiate the cleansing of the society from hard-liner communists and informers.<ref name=Ulrich1999/> He stated his aim as defense minister to transform the ministry into "an integrated civilian-military institution".<ref>{{cite book|author1=Natalie Mychajlyszyn|author2=Harald Von Riekhoff|title=The Evolution of Civil-military Relations in East-Central Europe and the Former Soviet Union|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IYApYztRK1wC&pg=PA52|year=2004|publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group|isbn=978-0-313-31562-6|page=52}}</ref> During his tenure Baudyš was informed that the Czech army had had [[pathogens]].<ref name=wh2009/> He ordered the destruction of them due to the fact that they were no longer necessary.<ref name=wh2009>{{cite book|author1=Mark Wheelis|author2=Lajos Rózsa|title=Deadly Cultures: Biological Weapons since 1945|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fj7aU0qzTLYC&pg=PA162|year=2009|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-04513-2|page=162}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Baudyš married twice. He had two sons from his first marriage.<ref name=eiwire/> In May 2010, he divorced his first wife and married a woman who was 23 years younger than him.<ref name=eiwire/>

He died at age 63 on 24 August 2010.<ref name=eiwire>{{cite news|title=Baudys held high posts in Czechoslovak, Czech govts in 1990s|url=http://www.accessmylibrary.com/article-1G1-235619535/baudys-held-high-posts.html|work=Europe Intelligence Wire|date=24 August 2010|agency=Czech News Agency|location=Prague}}</ref>
